title: As political pressure prompts exodus of Minnesota prosecutors, some defendants catch a break
text:
• The federal prosecutor’s office in Minnesota has experienced a wave of resignations and retirements.
• Cory Allen McKay, a 12-time convicted felon, had his methamphetamine trafficking charges dropped after the prosecutor on his case retired.
• The exodus of prosecutors is attributed to objections to Trump administration directives and the perceived politicization of decision-making.
• The number of assistant U.S. attorneys in Minnesota has fallen from over 40 to fewer than two dozen.
• The departures began last year, with prosecutors citing concerns about changes under the new administration.
• The office has been forced to dismiss cases, seek plea agreements, and request delays due to diminished resources.
• Local officials express concern about the office's ability to prosecute serious offenders.
• McKay's case involved charges related to a package of methamphetamine discovered in 2024.
• McKay has a history of violent crime, including strangulation and assault.
• The U.S. Attorney’s Office dropped McKay's case after the prosecutor, Thomas Hollenhorst, retired.
• McKay was released from jail on January 31.
• The office also dropped cases against other drug trafficking defendants.
summary: With a three-decade record of violent crime that includes strangling a pregnant woman and firing a shotgun under a person's chin, McKay was scheduled to stand trial next month on methamphetamine trafficking charges that could have locked him up for 25 years. “The result will be a diminished ability to target dangerous fraudsters, sexual predators, violent gangs and drug traffickers,” said John Marti, a Minneapolis lawyer who was a longtime fraud prosecutor in the office until 2015.
